newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian National sees revenues up 2.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Canadian National sees revenues up 2.2 pct.

text.p: Canadian National Railway Co is on track to improving its fiscal performance in coming years as revenues are forecast to grow above 2.2 percent a year while North America's sixth largest railway trims staff and sheds track, the firm's president and chief executive said.

"I don't think any company in Canada has changed as much as we have over the last three years and I don't think that any North American railroad has changed as much as we have in the last three years," CN president and chief executive Paul Tellier told reporters at a briefing here Tuesday.

Tellier was in Winnipeg to open CN's customer response center. Canada ships 40 percent of its exports by train and CN is the nation's largest railway company with revenues of C$4.1 billion in fiscal 1995.

"Longer term, we are going to grow the revenue line roughly by the equivalent of GDP (gross domestic product) and as you know the consensus on GDP for the U.S. is 2.2 percent and Canada is slightly higher than that," Tellier said.
Second quarter earnings per share in fiscal 1996 reached C$1.47 compared to C$1.15 in the same period in 1995. Standard and Poors has assigned the firm a triple-B rating.
Tellier said the third quarter, which ended Monday, did not see as high a return due to a significant drop in grain loading in that period but he did not have earnings figures.

"We should be growing the business, along the top (revenue) line more or less along (GDP). In terms of the expense line, we are right on target. The downsizing, the bulk of it is behind us," Tellier said.
The 160-year-old railway trimmed 11,000 staff in the past three years ending December 31, 1995, he said.
"We will be taking between 1,500 to 1,700 people off the payroll," Tellier said.
CN is also divesting itself of 2,000 miles of track this year with plans to shed at least another 2,000 and maybe up to 4,000 miles by the year 2000, he said.
Goods and services will be another source of cost saving for the carrier which spends C$1.5 billion a year on sourcing.
"I'm determined to cut this by 10 percent in the coming years. This year we will be cutting this by 30 percent and on October 1 we're right on target," Tellier said.
CN also plans to redefine the operations of its in-house research and consulting firm CANAC and an announcement should be made before the end of the year, Tellier said.
The firm did C$475 million-worth of business in 1995.

"CANAC is going to be refocused and is going to get out of many lines of business. We are the only railroad still doing in-house research. This is being examined and we are very close to making an announcement," Tellier said.
Operating costs in Ontario and east may be curtailed further if an agreement on the use of assets can be forged with CN's main rival, CP Rail System, a unit of Canadian Pacific Ltd, he said.
"Conversations are taking place between ourselves and CP Ltd on this," Tellier said.
"It is premature for me to say whether something will come out of it," he added.
